text: This is Cixa: a local checkout firewall between your software agents and real money. Here is how to connect an agent, set its limits, approve a purchase, and keep the payment boundary under your control.

Start with Docker. Clone Cixa, enter the repository, then run the owner stack. Ask for the dashboard token and open the loopback address. The console stays on this computer. Your agent never receives its token or owner access.

In Agents, create one capability for each runtime. Give it a clear name, keep the first mode at approval required, and set hard per-purchase, session, daily, and lifetime limits. Cixa writes the secret into its private agent volume. The browser only shows the filename.

Next, install the Cixa payment skill. It teaches Codex and Claude the purchase contract and the no-retry rules. Then register the disposable Cixa MCP container with the capability filename. The bridge has no network and cannot read owner state, card data, or dashboard credentials.

Start a fresh agent session with a safe connection check. Ask for Cixa status, capabilities, and remaining budget, without making a purchase. A connected agent reports only its own mode and limits. It should never ask for your card, KOHO login, or owner token.

When an agent reaches checkout, it sends the exact merchant, total, items, redirects, and consent facts to Cixa. Today shows what is waiting, what was spent, and what remains. Open an intent to inspect the bound facts, then allow that exact purchase once or decline it. Approval is never inferred from chat.

Trust is where the sensitive side stays deliberate. Configure the KOHO reference, approve a merchant-specific checkout profile, and open a short card session only when needed. Card details live only in the expiring helper process. They are not written to Cixa state, logs, receipts, or the agent.

After approval, the agent executes the intent once. Cixa rechecks the live checkout, reserves the amount before submission, and uses its isolated browser profile. If the result is uncertain, it stops instead of retrying. Check the transaction in KOHO, then record the provider outcome in Cixa.

That is the whole boundary: the agent shops, Cixa authorizes and submits, and you control authority and settlement. Start in approval-required mode, keep the limits small, and expand autonomy only after you trust the complete flow.
